title: ESS-Flow: Training-free guidance as Bayesian inference in source space
topic: Probabilistic Methods->Monte Carlo and Sampling Methods
claim: Sampling a Gaussian source space with ellipse moves maps through the flow to regions of high potential in data space.
layout: 2 panels, left-to-right, curved arrow labeled T_theta, formula banner on top
description: A formula banner at the top reads π(z) ∝ N(0, I) g(T_θ(z)), followed by a gray block arrow pointing to the label "ESS – Flow". Below it, on the left, is a large light-blue circle labeled "source p(z)". Inside it is a dashed purple ellipse with two yellow dots, marked ν and z_i. A curved black arrow labeled T_θ leads to the right panel, labeled "data p_θ(x)". There, an irregular pink blob holds a deformed dashed purple loop, which is the ellipse transformed by T_θ. A green elongated shape labeled "potential g(x)" overlaps the blob. The sample point x_i lies in the overlap, where the transformed ellipse passes through the high-potential region. Colors encode the distributions: blue for source, red for data, green for potential. The eye goes first to the circle and the ellipse.
caption: Illustration of ESS-Flow. We sample the target distribution π(z) in the source space of flow-based models, which typically has a Gaussian prior p(z). This allows gradient-free sampling with elliptical slice sampling. At stationarity, the transformed ellipse passes through regions of high potential in the data space by construction.
abstract: Guiding pretrained flow-based generative models for conditional generation or to produce samples with desired target properties enables solving diverse tasks without retraining on paired data. We present ESS-Flow, a gradient-free method that leverages the Gaussian prior of the source distribution in flow-based models to perform Bayesian inference directly in the source space using elliptical slice sampling. ESS-Flow only requires forward passes through the generative model and observation process, making it applicable even when gradients are unavailable, such as with non-differentiable simulation-based observations or quantization in the generation process. We demonstrate its effectiveness on scientific applications including generating materials with target properties, protein backbone structures with improved designability, and synthesizable, drug-like molecules.
